clips.text_zh: Reminder to all AI toddlers: train AI on GPL-licensed code, then use it as a loophole to generate that code back. Using current AI models for writing code may be license laundering. Your skills at asking AI nicely and clicking generate do not make you the author of its output. 靠AI續命都要識睇 licence。
clips.text_en_b1: Reminder to all AI toddlers: train AI on GPL-licensed code, then use it as a loophole to generate that code back. Everyone using current AI models to write code may be participating in license laundering. Your ability to ask AI nicely and click “generate” does not make you the author of the output. The original author may still own the rights.
clips.source_hint: The post argues that training AI on GPL code and generating it back is license laundering.

signal.rationale: This is a discussion about AI code licensing, not a trade.

clips.text_en_b2: A reminder for all AI toddlers: train a model on GPL-licensed code, then exploit the loophole by asking it to generate that same code back. In other words, using current AI models to write code may amount to license laundering rather than creating original work. Your talent for prompting an AI politely and clicking “generate” does not automatically make you the author of its output.
clips.text_en_c1: A reminder to all AI toddlers: train a model on GPL-licensed code, then exploit that as a loophole to have it generate the very same code back. Everyone who uses current AI models to write code may, in effect, be participating in licence laundering, since the underlying training material was never freely licensed for such reuse. Your talent for phrasing a request politely and clicking "generate" does not make you the author of the output, and the original author may very well retain the rights to it. Reading the licence is the part most people skip.
clips.text_en_c2: A reminder to all self-proclaimed AI toddlers: one can train a model on GPL-licensed code and then exploit the resulting system as a loophole to reproduce code of the same kind. In that sense, using contemporary AI models to write software may constitute licence laundering rather than legitimate authorship. The ability to formulate a polished request, click “generate,” and paste the result does not make a person the author of the output; intellectual property does not transfer merely because a machine produced the text. The original author may still own the relevant rights, so checking the licence remains indispensable.

clips.text_zh: Why wasn’t Asia politically relevant on the world stage until the 19th century? 香港咁細又咁逼，歷史上有冇可能根本唔係所謂「無地方住」？有啲問題由國家同航道決定，唔係淨係人口密度。
clips.text_en_b1: Why wasn’t Asia politically relevant on the world stage until the 19th century? The question points to a major historical change in regional power. For someone in Hong Kong, it also raises a broader issue: space, trade routes, and state power may matter more than population density alone.
clips.source_hint: The post asks why Asia became politically relevant on the world stage only in the 19th century.

signal.rationale: This is a historical discussion, not a market trade.

clips.text_en_b2: Why did Asia only become politically relevant on the world stage in the 19th century? The question points to a major historical shift in regional power, although the full explanation is obviously more complicated than a single cause. For someone living in Hong Kong, it also raises a broader issue: limited space, strategic trade routes, and the strength of the state may matter more than population density alone. In other words, countries can be squeezed geographically while still possessing enormous economic and political importance.
clips.text_en_c1: Why was it not until the 19th century that Asia became politically relevant on the world stage? The question points to a major shift in the regional balance of power rather than to any single invention or accident of history. For someone living in Hong Kong, it raises a broader issue that is easy to overlook: space, trade routes, and the reach of the state may matter considerably more than raw population density. Being hemmed in by geography and constrained by where the shipping lanes run can shape a region's prospects long before outsiders begin to notice.
clips.text_en_c2: Why did Asia appear to lack political relevance on the world stage until the nineteenth century? The question points to a profound transformation in the balance of regional power rather than a sudden awakening among populous societies. For someone living in Hong Kong, it also invites a broader reconsideration of the familiar claim that overcrowding alone determines a place’s historical importance. Some of Asia’s most consequential developments have hinged on statecraft, maritime access, trade routes, and the ability to command commercial networks. Geography and institutional capacity may therefore have mattered more than raw population density.

clips.text_en_b1: Deadlifts, squats, bench presses, pull-ups, and kettlebell swings: is this really all you need? The post proposes a simple strength routine built around four basic exercises. Fewer movements could save time, but proper form would still matter for the back, knees, and shoulders.

signal.rationale: This is a fitness discussion, not a trade.

clips.text_en_b2: Deadlifts, squats, bench presses, pull-ups, and kettlebell swings: is this really all you need? The post proposes a simple strength routine built around four basic exercises, with the ranking showing deadlifts first and swings last. Although fewer movements could save considerable time at the gym, beginners should not treat that efficiency as permission to ignore technique. Your back, knees, and shoulders need to be handled carefully, because doing the right exercises with sloppy form can still lead to injury rather than meaningful progress.
clips.text_en_c1: Deadlifts, squats, bench presses, pull-ups, and kettlebell swings: is this genuinely all you need? The post proposes a stripped-down strength routine built around four basic exercises, on the reasonable assumption that a beginner who trains consistently across those movements will get further than someone who endlessly cycles through variations without progressing. Fewer exercises certainly save time, which is a genuine advantage for anyone with a job and a limited schedule. That said, form is not negotiable: the back, the knees, and the shoulders are precisely where sloppy technique tends to announce itself first.
clips.text_en_c2: Deadlifts, squats, bench presses, pull-ups, and kettlebell swings: is this genuinely all that is needed? The post proposes an unfashionably simple strength programme built around four basic movements, with the kettlebell swing apparently relegated to fifth place. Such a streamlined routine could reclaim a substantial amount of time at the gym and spare beginners the confusion of chasing an endless catalogue of exercises. Nevertheless, efficiency must not come at the expense of technique. The back, knees, and shoulders remain vulnerable when even fundamental lifts are performed carelessly, so disciplined form is non-negotiable.

clips.text_en_b1: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a legacy on the anime industry? It feels like it sits between classic status and a normal popular show. The post asks whether an older series can still shape the industry without being one of the biggest mainstream names.
clips.source_hint: The post discusses Steins;Gate’s possible legacy within the anime industry.

signal.rationale: This is an anime discussion, not a trade.

clips.text_en_b2: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It feels as though it occupies an unusual space between genuine classic status and an ordinary popular show, rather than belonging comfortably in either category. The post asks whether an older series can continue to influence the industry without ever becoming one of the biggest mainstream names.
clips.text_en_c1: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It has always seemed to sit in an awkward category, somewhere between recognised classic status and an ordinary popular show that nobody outside the genre quite knows. The post raises a question worth taking seriously: can an older series still shape the medium it belongs to without ever becoming one of the biggest mainstream names? Perhaps the answer is that influence and visibility are not the same thing at all. Some of the most influential work only becomes obvious a decade later, once enough time has passed for it to be properly understood.
clips.text_en_c2: Do you think Steins;Gate has left a lasting legacy on the anime industry? It occupies an intriguing middle ground between an acknowledged classic and an ordinary popular programme: neither a mainstream commercial titan nor a disposable piece of fan culture. Yet influence is not synonymous with current popularity, and some anime acquire their stature slowly, acquiring new audiences and new critical recognition a decade after their initial release. The question therefore asks whether an older series can continue to shape the industry without belonging among its biggest household names, with Steins;Gate serving as the likely example.

clips.text_en_c2: Shibou Yuugi de Meshi wo Kuu, or “Playing Death Games to Put Food on the Table,” is still burning to this day, and a second season has now been announced. Its endurance suggests that the concept has outlasted the novelty of its premise and acquired a committed audience. One can sob over each episode while still recognising that, in purely cost-effective terms, it delivers considerable entertainment for very little.
